part_title: Classification Evaluation — Confusion Matrices, Precision, Recall and ROC
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 slides 46–49 visually inspected; diagrams, examples, labels and calculations reviewed against the approved beginner visual-first narration standard.

scenes.title: Binary classification: worked example
scenes.narration: We are now evaluating a classification model, not simply asking whether it can produce a label. Start on the left with a spam detector. Each incoming email is either truly spam or truly not spam. The model also predicts spam or not spam, but a prediction may be right or wrong. Move to the central confusion matrix. Read the rows as the actual category and the columns as the predicted category. When an email really is spam and the model says spam, that is a true positive, or T P. When spam is incorrectly marked not spam, that is a false negative, or F N: the harmful message slipped through. On the bottom row, a legitimate email that is incorrectly flagged as spam is a false positive, or F P, and a legitimate email correctly allowed through is a true negative, or T N. These four cases matter because different mistakes have different costs. Look to the right. Precision asks: of all emails we predicted as spam, how many really were spam? Its formula is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Recall asks: of all the emails that actually were spam, how many did we catch? Its denominator is true positives plus false negatives. A filter that marks everything spam may catch nearly all spam but also wrongly block important messages. A filter that flags only obvious spam may have high precision but let much spam through. The threshold and business requirements decide which error matters more. Quick check: if an important genuine invoice goes into the spam folder, is that a false negative? No. Because it was actually not spam but predicted spam, it is a false positive. Read the matrix position before choosing a metric.

scenes.title: Confusion Matrix
scenes.narration: On this slide the central confusion matrix gets a closer look. The left example uses a spam message saying you won a prize and a legitimate message about tomorrow's meeting. In this setup we define spam as the positive class, so not spam is the negative class. Positive does not mean good, and negative does not mean bad; these are names for the class the model is attempting to detect. Follow the diagram columns: predicted spam, then predicted not spam. Follow the rows: actual spam, then actual not spam. At the upper left a true positive is a spam message correctly caught. Upper right is a false negative, or missed spam. Lower left is a false positive, which means a legitimate message was blocked. Lower right is a true negative, which means a legitimate message was handled correctly. Now read the right-hand evaluation metrics. Precision is T P divided by T P plus F P. Recall is T P divided by T P plus F N. F one score combines precision and recall using two times their product divided by their sum; if both are zero, define the score appropriately rather than dividing by zero. Accuracy is T P plus T N divided by all four outcomes. Accuracy can be misleading when one class is extremely rare. Imagine nine hundred ninety legitimate messages and ten spam messages. A detector predicting not spam for every email is ninety-nine percent accurate but catches no spam. The right metric depends on the actual goal. If missing dangerous messages is expensive, prioritize recall while controlling false alarms. If blocking a legitimate business message is costly, inspect precision and false positives. The bottom takeaway is to consider error types, not only a single headline score.

scenes.title: Multiclass confusion matrices
scenes.narration: The previous two slides dealt with exactly two possible labels. Now this image shows three: cat, dog and bird. Start on the left with the three animal photographs entering a classification model. The model produces one of the three categories. The middle grid is a multiclass confusion matrix. In this slide, rows show the actual class and columns show the predicted class. A cat correctly predicted as cat appears on the diagonal, as do dog as dog and bird as bird. A true dog predicted as cat is recorded in the dog row and cat column. That off-diagonal entry is a mistake. Each cell would contain a count of predictions in a real evaluation; this visual illustrates the categories rather than showing actual counts. Notice how the grid reveals which animals the model confuses. Maybe dogs are mistaken for cats more often than birds, and that would direct us to check training examples or image quality. On the right we see precision, recall, F one and accuracy again. In multiclass problems, we can compute precision and recall for each class using one-versus-rest thinking, and then combine results using macro or weighted averaging. Macro averaging gives each class similar importance; weighted averaging reflects how many examples belong to each class. An overall accuracy number may hide terrible performance on a rare category. The best metric depends on whether missing one class carries greater cost. Quick example: if a true bird is labeled dog, should the dog count as a correctly identified dog? No. It is an error in the bird row and dog prediction column. Remember: diagonal means correct for this diagram; off diagonal means confusion.

scenes.title: ROC curves: worked example
scenes.narration: This slide illustrates receiver operating characteristic curves, usually called R O C curves. The example at the left is fraud detection. A model outputs scores interpreted here as fraud probabilities: transaction A is actually fraud with score zero point nine two, B is legitimate with zero point eight zero, C is fraud with zero point six five, D is legitimate with zero point four zero, E is fraud with zero point three zero and F is legitimate with zero point one zero. These are small teaching data, not a realistic benchmark. A decision threshold turns a score into a fraud alert. Lowering that threshold usually catches more fraudulent cases but also flags more legitimate purchases. The R O C chart plots false positive rate along the horizontal axis and true positive rate along the vertical axis at different thresholds. True positive rate is recall. False positive rate is false positives divided by false positives plus true negatives. Look at the middle graphs. The poor model's orange curve stays near the dashed diagonal, suggesting ranking only slightly better than random guessing. The good model's blue curve bends toward the upper-left corner, meaning it achieves more true positives for relatively few false positives. The last comparison overlays both curves. Area under the curve, or A U C, summarizes ranking performance across thresholds; a larger R O C A U C usually means better discrimination for the same evaluation data. But A U C is not the same as classification accuracy and does not show whether probability estimates are well calibrated. With highly imbalanced fraud datasets, precision-recall curves can also provide useful context. Check your understanding: when a company wants fewer wrongful fraud alerts, should it look only at overall accuracy? No. It should examine false positive rates, precision, recall and thresholds alongside the business cost.
